exercises.approach: Compute each group's mean and sd with the n minus 1 divisor, then divide sd by the square root of its own count, 4.
exercises.why: A = 1, 2, 3, 4 has mean 2.5 and squared deviations summing to 5, so the variance is 5/3 and SE squared is 5/12. B = 2, 3, 6, 7 has mean 4.5 and squared deviations summing to 17, so SE squared is 17/12.
exercises.wrong: Dividing the squared deviations by n instead of n minus 1. A would then get SE squared 5/16 instead of 5/12, a quarter smaller in variance and too narrow in every interval built from it.

exercises.approach: Multiply each SE by qt(0.975, 3), about 3.18, and add and subtract that half width from each mean.
exercises.why: Each group has 4 values and so 3 degrees of freedom. A's half width is about 2.05, giving 0.45 to 4.55, and B's is about 3.79, giving 0.71 to 8.29.
exercises.wrong: Using the normal value 1.96. With 3 degrees of freedom the half widths shrink by about 38 percent, to about 1.27 and 2.33, and the intervals claim more precision than four values support.
exercises.verify: `all(half > se)` returns TRUE, and `half` returns about 2.05 and 3.79.

exercises.approach: Compute one ylim from the raw values together with every interval endpoint and pass it to both panels.
exercises.why: The raw values span 1 to 7 but the intervals reach about 0.45 and 8.29, so the shared range is 0.45 to 8.29. A unit of height then means the same amount in both panels.
exercises.wrong: Taking limits from the raw values alone. B's upper end and A's lower end then fall outside 1 to 7, so their arrows are clipped and look shorter than they are.
exercises.verify: `range(c(unlist(groups), means - half, means + half))` returns about 0.45 and 8.29.

exercises.approach: Label the bars by what they are: draw the t interval and call it a 95 percent interval, or draw plus or minus one SE and call it that.
exercises.why: For these groups the t interval is qt(0.975, 3), about 3.18 times, wider than one SE. A's one SE bar would run 1.85 to 3.15, while its stated interval runs 0.45 to 4.55.
exercises.wrong: Drawing mean plus or minus SE and titling it 95 percent intervals. The bars are about a third of the stated width, so A and B look more clearly separated than the intervals allow.
exercises.verify: `half / se` returns about 3.18 for both groups.

exercises.approach: Check the values before plotting on a log axis, and decide openly how a zero or negative value will be handled.
exercises.why: log(0) is minus infinity, so zero has no position on the axis. For 1, 10 and 100 the log10 gaps are both 1, which is why those points sit equally spaced even though their raw differences are 9 and 90.
exercises.wrong: Letting plot drop the zero with only a warning, or adding 1 to every value. The shift turns 1, 10 and 100 into 2, 11 and 101, whose ratios are no longer equal, so the spacing changes meaning.
exercises.verify: `is.finite(log(0))` returns FALSE, and the log10 differences of `c(1, 10, 100)` return 1 and 1.

exercises.approach: Inside draw, save the result of par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = ...) and register `par(old)` with on.exit.
exercises.why: par returns the previous values of the settings it changes, so on.exit restores the caller's layout and margins when draw returns, even after an error. draw never closes the device, which belongs to the caller.
exercises.wrong: Ending the helper with dev.off to tidy up, which closes the caller's device, or never restoring mfrow, so the caller's next plot lands in half of the page.

run_note: The starter holds two groups of four observations, A with 1 to 4 and B with 2, 3, 6 and 7, and an empty results list. Run it and compute the means, 2.5 and 4.5, and the squared standard errors, 5/12 and 17/12, by hand. A 95 percent t interval with three degrees of freedom is much wider than one standard error, so label each bar with exactly what it shows.
checks_note: The checks confirm means of 2.5 and 4.5 with squared standard errors 5/12 and 17/12, interval half widths larger than one standard error, a restored `mfrow` layout after the helper returns, that the logarithm of zero is not finite, and that 1, 10 and 100 are equally spaced on a log10 axis. They do not show that the two groups differ, and they cannot check whether readers interpret the bars correctly.
